Select all that apply."] [:db/add "8f541e25-e4dd-5415-ad10-5dcd34f06844" :question/worked-solution "![](images/67/67ef97be4b21a74feaae15f3ff30d5077fc1316874df8de79155316a621e4487.png)

Recall the following:

- $N$ represents the set of **natural numbers**.

- $Z$ represents the set of **integers**.

- $Q$ represents the set of **rational numbers**.

- $R$ represents the set of **real numbers**.

- $C$ represents the set of **complex numbers**.

With that in mind, we note the following:

- First, we note that $\sqrt{-83}=\sqrt{83}\text{i}$ is a complex number. Therefore, we can write

$$
\sqrt{-83}\in C
$$

- Since the imaginary part of $\sqrt{-83}$ is nonzero, it does *not* belong to $N,Z,Q,$ or $R.$ We can write

$$
\begin{gathered}\sqrt{-83}\notin N\qquad \sqrt{-83}\notin Z \\ \sqrt{-83}\notin Q\qquad \sqrt{-83}\notin R\end{gathered}
$$

Recall the following:

- $N$ represents the set of **natural numbers**.

- $Z$ represents the set of **integers**.

- $Q$ represents the set of **rational numbers**.

- $R$ represents the set of **real numbers**.

- $C$ represents the set of **complex numbers**.

With that in mind, we note the following:

- The number $\sqrt{58}$ is not an integer, so it does *not* belong to $Z$ nor to $N.$ We can write

$$
\sqrt{58}\notin N\qquad \sqrt{58}\notin Z
$$

- Also, $\sqrt{58}$ is irrational because $58$ is positive and not a perfect square. It cannot be written as the ratio of two integers, so it does *not* belong to $Q$ either:

$$
\sqrt{58}\notin Q
$$

- Every irrational number is both a real number and a complex number. Consequently, $\sqrt{58}$ belongs to both $R$ and $C,$ and we can write

$$
\sqrt{58}\in R\qquad \sqrt{58}\in C
$$

Select all that apply."] [:db/add "cdc66198-5eb8-5264-9ff6-2849efaaf195" :question/worked-solution "![](images/67/67ef97be4b21a74feaae15f3ff30d5077fc1316874df8de79155316a621e4487.png)

Recall the following:

- $N$ represents the set of **natural numbers**.

- $Z$ represents the set of **integers**.

- $Q$ represents the set of **rational numbers**.

- $R$ represents the set of **real numbers**.

- $C$ represents the set of **complex numbers**.

With that in mind, we note the following:

- The number $14$ is a positive whole number, so it belongs to $N.$ We can write

$$
14\in N
$$

- Every natural number is an integer, rational, real, and complex number. Consequently, we can write

$$
\begin{gathered}14\in Z\qquad 14\in Q \\ 14\in R\qquad 14\in C\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $N, Z, Q, R, C$."] [:db/add "cdc66198-5eb8-5264-9ff6-2849efaaf195" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [:db/add "cdc66198-5eb8-5264-9ff6-2849efaaf195" $$

$$
\sqrt{58}\notin Q
$$

- Every irrational number is both a real number and a complex number. Consequently, $\sqrt{58}$ belongs to both $R$ and $C,$ and we can write

$$
\sqrt{58}\in R\qquad \sqrt{58}\in C
$$

- The number $\sqrt{58}$ is not an integer, so it does *not* belong to $Z$ nor to $N.$ We can write

$$
\sqrt{58}\notin N\qquad \sqrt{58}\notin Z
$$

- Also, $\sqrt{58}$ is irrational because $58$ is positive and not a perfect square. It cannot be written as the ratio of two integers, so it does *not* belong to $Q$ either:

$$
\sqrt{58}\notin Q
$$

- Every irrational number is both a real number and a complex number. Consequently, $\sqrt{58}$ belongs to both $R$ and $C,$ and we can write

$$
\sqrt{58}\in R\qquad \sqrt{58}\in C
$$
